user_input: In DRF, when exactly do the authentication classes run relative to the rest of my view logic?
reference: Authentication is the very first thing a DRF view does. It runs before the permission and throttling checks and before any of your own view code.
reference_contexts: Authentication always runs at the very start of the view, before the permission and throttling checks occur, and before any other code is allowed to proceed.

user_input: Coming from plain Django I keep hunting for some kind of "login middleware" I can switch on so the whole API requires auth — but there doesn't seem to be one. What's the DRF way to set the authentication for every endpoint at once?
reference: Set them globally with DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES in your REST_FRAMEWORK settings dict; every view uses that default unless it overrides it per-view or per-viewset.
reference_contexts: The default authentication schemes may be set globally, using the DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES setting.

REST_FRAMEWORK = { 'DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES' : [ 'rest_framework.authentication.BasicAuthentication' , 'rest_framework.authentication.SessionAuthentication' , ] } You can also set the authentication scheme on a per-view or per-viewset basis, using the APIView class-based views.

user_input: What header and prefix does DRF's built-in TokenAuthentication expect for the token?
reference: Send it in the Authorization header prefixed with the literal word "Token" and a space, e.g. `Authorization: Token 9944...`. Subclass TokenAuthentication if you'd rather use a keyword like Bearer.
reference_contexts: key ) For clients to authenticate, the token key should be included in the Authorization HTTP header.

For example: Authorization : Token 9944b09199c62bcf9418ad846dd0e4bbdfc6ee4b If you want to use a different keyword in the header, such as Bearer , simply subclass TokenAuthentication and set the keyword class variable.

user_input: Which permission class gives anonymous users read access but requires login to write?
reference: IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly: authenticated users can make any request, while unauthenticated users are limited to the safe methods GET, HEAD and OPTIONS.
reference_contexts: The IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly will allow authenticated users to perform any request.
This permission is suitable if you want to your API to allow read permissions to anonymous users, and only allow write permissions to authenticated users.

user_input: What's the difference between IsAuthenticated and AllowAny?
reference: IsAuthenticated blocks anonymous users and lets logged-in users through; AllowAny lets every request through regardless of authentication.
reference_contexts: The IsAuthenticated permission class will deny permission to any unauthenticated user, and allow permission otherwise.
The AllowAny permission class will allow unrestricted access, regardless of if the request was authenticated or unauthenticated .

user_input: How do I turn on pagination for my whole API, and what settings does it need?
reference: Set DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS and PAGE_SIZE globally in REST_FRAMEWORK. You need both — they're None by default.
reference_contexts: The pagination style may be set globally, using the DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS and PAGE_SIZE setting keys.

For example, to use the built-in limit/offset pagination, you would do something like this: REST_FRAMEWORK = { 'DEFAULT_PAGINATION_CLASS' : 'rest_framework.pagination.LimitOffsetPagination' , 'PAGE_SIZE' : 100 } Note that you need to set both the pagination class, and the page size that should be used.

user_input: I added a pagination class but my list endpoint won't paginate. Does pagination work with any view?
reference: Only generic views and viewsets paginate automatically. A plain APIView won't unless you call the pagination API yourself.
reference_contexts: Pagination is only performed automatically if you're using the generic views or viewsets.

user_input: What do I set so clients can search my list endpoint with ?search=?
reference: Add DRF's SearchFilter to the view and give it a search_fields attribute; the filter only activates once search_fields is set.
reference_contexts: When in use, the browsable API will include a SearchFilter control: The SearchFilter class will only be applied if the view has a search_fields attribute set.
The search_fields attribute should be a list of names of text type fields on the model, such as CharField or TextField .

user_input: How do I let clients order list results but restrict which fields they can sort on?
reference: Use OrderingFilter and set an explicit ordering_fields list on the view so users can't sort on sensitive columns.
reference_contexts: It's recommended that you explicitly specify which fields the API should allow in the ordering filter.
You can do this by setting an ordering_fields attribute on the view, like so: class UserListView ( generics .

user_input: I've got a Spring background and I'm looking for DRF's equivalent of a DTO — something to turn a list of model objects into JSON in one shot. How do I serialize a whole queryset at once?
reference: Pass many=True when instantiating the serializer, then give it the queryset or list of objects.
reference_contexts: To serialize a queryset or list of objects instead of a single object instance, you should pass the many=True flag when instantiating the serializer.

user_input: Instead of marking every field read_only=True individually on my ModelSerializer, is there a shortcut?
reference: Yes — use the Meta option read_only_fields with a list/tuple of field names.
reference_contexts: You may wish to specify multiple fields as read-only.

ModelSerializer ): class Meta : model = Account fields = [ 'id' , 'account_name' , 'users' , 'created' ] read_only_fields = [ 'account_name' ] Model fields which have editable=False set, and AutoField fields will be set to read-only by default, and do not need to be added to the read_only_fields option.

user_input: What does the depth option on a ModelSerializer Meta control?
reference: How many levels of relationships get expanded into nested representations before DRF reverts to a flat (primary-key) representation.
reference_contexts: ModelSerializer ): class Meta : model = Account fields = [ 'id' , 'account_name' , 'users' , 'created' ] depth = 1 The depth option should be set to an integer value that indicates the depth of relationships that should be traversed before reverting to a flat representation.

user_input: What does serializer.is_valid(raise_exception=True) do?
reference: It raises a serializers.ValidationError on invalid data, which DRF's default exception handler turns into a 400 response automatically.
reference_contexts: The .is_valid() method takes an optional raise_exception flag that will cause it to raise a serializers.ValidationError exception if there are validation errors.

user_input: Where do I put validation for a single serializer field?
reference: Add a .validate_<field_name> method to your Serializer subclass — it works like Django forms' .clean_<field_name> and gets the field value.
reference_contexts: You can specify custom field-level validation by adding .validate_<field_name> methods to your Serializer subclass.

user_input: Which validator enforces a model's unique=True at the serializer level?
reference: UniqueValidator — attach it to the serializer field with the queryset to check against.
reference_contexts: This validator can be used to enforce the unique=True constraint on model fields.
This validator should be applied to serializer fields , like so: from rest_framework .

user_input: What's a SerializerMethodField for?
reference: A read-only field whose value comes from a method on the serializer, letting you add arbitrary computed data to the output.
reference_contexts: This is a read-only field. It gets its value by calling a method on the serializer class it is attached to.

user_input: What does write_only=True on a field do?
reference: It makes the field usable for create/update but keeps it out of serialized output — handy for passwords.
reference_contexts: Set this to True to ensure that the field may be used when updating or creating an instance, but is not included when serializing the representation.

user_input: How does the source argument on a serializer field work?
reference: source names the attribute used to populate the field; it can be a no-arg method or a dotted path like 'user.email' to traverse relations.
reference_contexts: The name of the attribute that will be used to populate the field.

user_input: What's the simplest related field to render a relation using the target's __str__?
reference: StringRelatedField, which represents the target via its __str__ method and is read-only.
reference_contexts: StringRelatedField may be used to represent the target of the relationship using its __str__ method.

user_input: How do I represent a relation by a unique field on the related object instead of its PK?
reference: Use SlugRelatedField and set slug_field to the attribute you want to represent it by.
reference_contexts: SlugRelatedField may be used to represent the target of the relationship using a field on the target.

user_input: Which parser accepts multipart form data with file uploads?
reference: MultiPartParser; pair it with FormParser to fully support HTML form data.
reference_contexts: Parses multipart HTML form content, which supports file uploads.
You will typically want to use both FormParser and MultiPartParser together in order to fully support HTML form data.

user_input: In tests, how do I authenticate a request without the real credential flow?
reference: Use force_authenticate() to directly authenticate the request against a user (and optionally a token).
reference_contexts: To forcibly authenticate a request, use the force_authenticate() method.

user_input: Why prefer request.query_params over request.GET in DRF?
reference: request.query_params is DRF's more correctly named synonym for request.GET; it's clearer since any HTTP method can carry query parameters.
reference_contexts: For clarity inside your code, we recommend using request.query_params instead of the Django's standard request.GET .

user_input: What's DRF's reverse() and how does it differ from Django's?
reference: rest_framework.reverse.reverse behaves like django.urls.reverse but returns a fully qualified URL using the request's host/port — so pass the request.
reference_contexts: Signature: reverse(viewname, *args, **kwargs) Has the same behavior as django.urls.reverse , except that it returns a fully qualified URL, using the request to determine the host and port.

user_input: What does @api_view do to a plain function view?
reference: It wraps the function so it gets a DRF Request and returns a DRF Response for the listed HTTP methods; by default only GET is accepted and others get a 405.
reference_contexts: By default only GET methods will be accepted. Other methods will respond with "405 Method Not Allowed".

user_input: We're launching a mobile app with ~200k users and we don't want server-side sessions. I want each user to authenticate once and then send some credential on every request, and I need an endpoint that hands that credential back given a username and password. What's the DRF-native approach and what do I have to install/migrate?
reference: TokenAuthentication fits client-server setups like mobile apps. Enable it plus rest_framework.authtoken, run migrate, and expose the built-in obtain_auth_token view so clients POST username/password and get a token to send in the Authorization header.
reference_contexts: Token authentication is appropriate for client-server setups, such as native desktop and mobile clients.
REST framework provides a built-in view to provide this behavior.

The obtain_auth_token view will return a JSON response when valid username and password fields are POSTed to the view using form data or JSON: { 'token' : '9944b09199c62bcf9418ad846dd0e4bbdfc6ee4b' } Note that the default obtain_auth_token view explicitly uses JSON requests and responses, rather than using default renderer and parser classes in your settings.
A list or tuple of authentication classes, that determines the default set of authenticators used when accessing the request.user or request.auth properties.

user_input: I want everyone to be able to browse my data, but only the user who created a record should be able to change or delete it. How do I structure this in DRF?
reference: Combine IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly with a custom object-level permission (IsOwnerOrReadOnly) whose has_object_permission allows safe methods for anyone and write methods only when obj.owner == request.user.
reference_contexts: BasePermission ): """ Custom permission to only allow owners of an object to edit it.
SAFE_METHODS : return True # Write permissions are only allowed to the owner of the snippet.
The IsAuthenticatedOrReadOnly will allow authenticated users to perform any request.

user_input: When a user creates a record, I want its owner set automatically to whoever is logged in — the client should never send it. What's the clean way?
reference: Don't take it from request data. In a generic view override perform_create to save with user=self.request.user, or on the serializer use a HiddenField with default=CurrentUserDefault so the current user is injected at save.
reference_contexts: These hooks are particularly useful for setting attributes that are implicit in the request, but are not part of the request data.
A default class that can be used to represent the current user.
This field will be present in validated_data but will not be used in the serializer output representation.

user_input: My API is getting hammered. I want to cap how many requests anonymous vs logged-in users can make per day. What's the mechanism and where do the numbers go?
reference: Enable AnonRateThrottle and UserRateThrottle as throttle classes and put the actual limits (like '100/day' and '1000/day') under DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES.
reference_contexts: The default throttling policy may be set globally, using the DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES and DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES settings.

REST_FRAMEWORK = { 'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_CLASSES' : [ 'rest_framework.throttling.AnonRateThrottle' , 'rest_framework.throttling.UserRateThrottle' ], 'DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES' : { 'anon' : '100/day' , 'user' : '1000/day' } } The rates used in DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES can be specified over a period of second, minute, hour or day.
A list or tuple of throttle classes, that determines the default set of throttles checked at the start of a view.

user_input: I need different rate limits for different parts of my API — a strict cap on uploads but looser on contacts. How do I do per-area limits rather than one global user rate?
reference: Use ScopedRateThrottle: give each view a .throttle_scope naming its area and set a rate per scope in DEFAULT_THROTTLE_RATES. The throttle only applies to views that declare a throttle_scope.
reference_contexts: The ScopedRateThrottle class can be used to restrict access to specific parts of the API.
This throttle will only be applied if the view that is being accessed includes a .throttle_scope property.
The unique throttle key will then be formed by concatenating the "scope" of the request with the unique user id or IP address.
A list or tuple of throttle classes, that determines the default set of throttles checked at the start of a view.

user_input: I want users to only ever see and edit their own objects through my list endpoints — never anyone else's. Recommended approach?
reference: Filter the queryset per request: override get_queryset to restrict results to request.user's objects, because object-level permissions aren't applied across a list for performance reasons.
reference_contexts: The simplest way to filter the queryset of any view that subclasses GenericAPIView is to override the .get_queryset() method.
You can do so by filtering based on the value of request.user .
For performance reasons the generic views will not automatically apply object level permissions to each instance in a queryset when returning a list of objects.
queryset - The queryset that should be used for returning objects from this view.

user_input: I want to accept a nested object in one POST — create a user together with their profile. Does DRF handle that out of the box?
reference: No. The default ModelSerializer create/update don't support writable nested representations, so you must write your own .create()/.update(), or use a package like DRF Writable Nested.
reference_contexts: The default ModelSerializer .create() and .update() methods do not include support for writable nested representations.
There are however, third-party packages available such as DRF Writable Nested that support automatic writable nested representations.

save () return instance Because the behavior of nested creates and updates can be ambiguous, and may require complex dependencies between related models, REST framework 3 requires you to always write these methods explicitly.
Such nested relationships can be expressed by using serializers as fields.

user_input: I want a self-describing API I can click around in a browser during development, with JSON still the primary format. How do I set that up?
reference: Register JSONRenderer and BrowsableAPIRenderer under DEFAULT_RENDERER_CLASSES. JSON stays primary while the browsable renderer shows an HTML page reusing the highest-priority renderer for the body.
reference_contexts: The default set of renderers may be set globally, using the DEFAULT_RENDERER_CLASSES setting.

Renders data into HTML for the Browsable API: This renderer will determine which other renderer would have been given highest priority, and use that to display an API style response within the HTML page.

REST_FRAMEWORK = { 'DEFAULT_RENDERER_CLASSES' : [ 'rest_framework.renderers.JSONRenderer' , 'rest_framework.renderers.BrowsableAPIRenderer' , ] } You can also set the renderers used for an individual view, or viewset, using the APIView class-based views.

REST framework uses a simple style of content negotiation to determine which media type should be returned to a client, based on the available renderers, the priorities of each of those renderers, and the client's Accept: header.

user_input: I'm tired of writing near-identical URL patterns for every model's list and detail views. What's the DRF way to cut that boilerplate?
reference: Move to ViewSets and let a router generate URLs: register each ViewSet with a router and include router.urls, which keeps URL conventions consistent and removes hand-written patterns.
reference_contexts: The conventions for wiring up resources into views and urls can be handled automatically, using a Router class.

It helps ensure that URL conventions will be consistent across your API, minimizes the amount of code you need to write, and allows you to concentrate on the interactions and representations your API provides rather than the specifics of the URL conf.

Also note that although this class provides the complete set of create/list/retrieve/update/destroy actions by default, you can restrict the available operations by using the standard permission classes.
REST framework adds support for automatic URL routing to Django, and provides you with a simple, quick and consistent way of wiring your view logic to a set of URLs.

user_input: My hyperlinked serializers produce relative, broken URLs. What am I missing to get full absolute URLs?
reference: HyperlinkedModelSerializer needs the current request in its context to build fully qualified URLs; pass context={'request': request} (generic views do this for you).
reference_contexts: When instantiating a HyperlinkedModelSerializer you must include the current request in the serializer context, for example: serializer = AccountSerializer ( queryset , context ={ 'request' : request }) Doing so will ensure that the hyperlinks can include an appropriate hostname, so that the resulting representation uses fully qualified URLs, such as: http : //api.example.com/accounts/1/ Rather than relative URLs, such as: /accounts/ 1 / If you do want to use relative URLs, you should explicitly pass {'request': None} in the serializer context.
HyperlinkedRelatedField may be used to represent the target of the relationship using a hyperlink.

user_input: I need to ship a v2 of my API that returns data differently from v1 without breaking existing clients. How does DRF support versioning the behavior of a view?
reference: Turn on a versioning scheme so request.version is available, then branch on it — e.g. return a different serializer class from get_serializer_class depending on the version.
reference_contexts: How you vary the API behavior is up to you, but one example you might typically want is to switch to a different serialization style in a newer version.

You can also set your versioning class plus those three values on a per-view or a per-viewset basis by defining your own versioning scheme and using the default_version , allowed_versions and version_param class variables.
Returns the class that should be used for the serializer.

user_input: I want to expose an extra custom action on a viewset — like a 'highlight' endpoint on a snippet — that the router routes for me. How?
reference: Mark the method with @action and set detail=True or detail=False to say whether it acts on a single object or the collection; the router then builds its URL.
reference_contexts: If you have ad-hoc methods that should be routable, you can mark them as such with the @action decorator.
To indicate this, set the detail argument to True or False .
Use the url_path and url_name parameters to change the URL segment and the reverse URL name of the action.
REST framework adds support for automatic URL routing to Django, and provides you with a simple, quick and consistent way of wiring your view logic to a set of URLs.

user_input: I've got a React front-end served from the same domain as my API. Users log in through the normal Django login page, but my fetch() POSTs randomly come back 403 while GETs work fine. Do I need JWT? CORS headers? Something with CSRF tokens? What's the right setup here?
reference: Use SessionAuthentication so same-context AJAX authenticates off the existing session — but include a valid CSRF token on unsafe methods like POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE.
reference_contexts: This ensures that once a user has logged in, any AJAX requests made can be authenticated using the same session-based authentication that is used for the rest of the website.

If you're using an AJAX-style API with SessionAuthentication, you'll need to make sure you include a valid CSRF token for any "unsafe" HTTP method calls, such as PUT , PATCH , POST or DELETE requests.

If you’re building a JavaScript client to interface with your Web API, you'll need to consider if the client can use the same authentication policy that is used by the rest of the website, and also determine if you need to use CSRF tokens or CORS headers.

user_input: I want some endpoints to render as real HTML pages using my own templates. What renderer supports that and what does the view return?
reference: TemplateHTMLRenderer: the view returns a dict of context data and names a template, and the renderer builds the HTML page — serializers can even act as HTML forms in those templates.
reference_contexts: The TemplateHTMLRenderer class expects the response to contain a dictionary of context data, and renders an HTML page based on a template that must be specified either in the view or on the response.
Additionally, serializers can be used as HTML forms and rendered in templates.
REST framework is suitable for returning both API style responses, and regular HTML pages.
Renders data to HTML, using Django's standard template rendering.

user_input: I want to accept a raw file upload from a native client streaming the file body, not a multipart form. How do I set up the parser and how does DRF get the filename?
reference: Use FileUploadParser, which puts the file at request.data['file']; the filename comes from a filename URL kwarg if present, otherwise the client sets it in Content-Disposition.
reference_contexts: The request.data property will be a dictionary with a single key 'file' containing the uploaded file.
If it is called without a filename URL keyword argument, then the client must set the filename in the Content-Disposition HTTP header.
.media_type : */* Note The FileUploadParser is for usage with native clients that can upload the file as a raw data request.
A list or tuple of parser classes, that determines the default set of parsers used when accessing the request.data property.

user_input: I want to combine two permission rules — e.g. authenticated OR a read-only request — without writing a whole new class. Is there a concise way?
reference: Yes: permission classes inheriting from BasePermission compose with Python's bitwise operators, so IsAuthenticated | ReadOnly works using &, | and ~.
reference_contexts: Provided they inherit from rest_framework.permissions.BasePermission , permissions can be composed using standard Python bitwise operators.

method in SAFE_METHODS class ExampleView ( APIView ): permission_classes = [ IsAuthenticated | ReadOnly ] def get ( self , request , format = None ): content = { 'status' : 'request was permitted' } return Response ( content ) Note Composition of permissions supports the & (and), | (or) and ~ (not) operators, and also allows the use of brackets ( ) to group expressions.
Operators follow the same precedence and associativity rules as standard logical operators ( ~ highest, then & , then | ).

user_input: Behind Apache with mod_wsgi, my token auth fails — the Authorization header seems to vanish. What's going on and how do I fix it at deploy level?
reference: mod_wsgi doesn't pass the Authorization header to the app by default, so non-session auth breaks. Set WSGIPassAuthorization to 'On' to forward it.
reference_contexts: Note that if deploying to Apache using mod_wsgi , the authorization header is not passed through to a WSGI application by default, as it is assumed that authentication will be handled by Apache, rather than at an application level.
This can be done by specifying the WSGIPassAuthorization directive in the appropriate context and setting it to 'On' .

user_input: I want clients to page through a huge, constantly-growing table efficiently and never see duplicates when rows are inserted mid-scroll. Which pagination style and what's the catch?
reference: CursorPagination: consistent, fixed-time paging that avoids duplicates even as rows are inserted, but it needs a unique, unchanging ordering and only allows forward/reverse navigation.
reference_contexts: Cursor based pagination requires that there is a unique, unchanging ordering of items in the result set.
This pagination style only presents forward and reverse controls, and does not allow the client to navigate to arbitrary positions.
With extremely large datasets pagination using offset-based pagination styles may become inefficient or unusable.
The default class to use for queryset pagination.

user_input: I want a rich, declarative way to let clients filter a list on multiple model fields via query params, beyond DRF's simple search. What integrates with DRF?
reference: Use django-filter's DjangoFilterBackend for highly customizable field filtering: install django-filter, add 'django_filters' to INSTALLED_APPS, and wire the backend via DEFAULT_FILTER_BACKENDS or per view.
reference_contexts: The django-filter library includes a DjangoFilterBackend class which supports highly customizable field filtering for REST framework.
To use DjangoFilterBackend , first install django-filter .

all () serializer_class = ProductSerializer filter_backends = [ DjangoFilterBackend ] filterset_fields = [ 'category' , 'in_stock' ] This will automatically create a FilterSet class for the given fields, and will allow you to make requests such as: http : //example.com/api/products?category=clothing&in_stock=True For more advanced filtering requirements you can specify a FilterSet class that should be used by the view.
A list of filter backend classes that should be used for generic filtering.

user_input: I want to stop a user creating two records with the same combination of two fields — like no two items sharing a position in the same list. How do I express that in DRF validation?
reference: Apply a UniqueTogetherValidator in the serializer's Meta.validators with the queryset and the field names that must be unique as a set; note it implicitly treats those fields as required.
reference_contexts: This validator can be used to enforce unique_together constraints on model instances.
fields required - A list or tuple of field names which should make a unique set.
all (), fields =[ 'list' , 'position' ] ) ] Note The UniqueTogetherValidator class always imposes an implicit constraint that all the fields it applies to are always treated as required.
Serializer classes can also include reusable validators that are applied to the complete set of field data.

user_input: I want my custom permission to return a specific, human-friendly denial message instead of DRF's generic one. How?
reference: Set a message attribute directly on your custom permission class; when the check fails DRF uses it instead of PermissionDenied's default_detail.
reference_contexts: To change the error message associated with the exception, implement a message attribute directly on your custom permission.
Otherwise the default_detail attribute from PermissionDenied will be used.

user_input: When should I reach for a ReadOnlyModelViewSet instead of a full ModelViewSet, and what do the two actually differ on?
reference: Use ReadOnlyModelViewSet when you only need read endpoints: it provides just .list() and .retrieve(), whereas ModelViewSet gives the full create/list/retrieve/update/destroy set. Both inherit from GenericAPIView and both still require queryset and serializer_class.
reference_contexts: all () serializer_class = UserSerializer Here we've used the ReadOnlyModelViewSet class to automatically provide the default 'read-only' operations.
We're still setting the queryset and serializer_class attributes exactly as we did when we were using regular views, but we no longer need to provide the same information to two separate classes.
The ModelViewSet class inherits from GenericAPIView and includes implementations for various actions, by mixing in the behavior of the various mixin classes.
The ReadOnlyModelViewSet class also inherits from GenericAPIView .

user_input: During tests I want to exercise my views like a client would — hitting URLs with get/post/put and JSON bodies — not building requests by hand. What does DRF give me?
reference: APIClient, which extends Django's test Client and supports the same .get()/.post()/.put()/.patch()/.delete()/.head()/.options() interface.
reference_contexts: The APIClient class supports the same request interface as Django's standard Client class.
This means that the standard .get() , .post() , .put() , .patch() , .delete() , .head() and .options() methods are all available.

user_input: I want to read one of DRF's effective settings (like the default auth classes) from my own code, respecting any overrides. What object should I use?
reference: Import api_settings from rest_framework.settings and read the attribute; it checks user-defined settings first, falls back to defaults, and auto-imports classes referenced by string path.
reference_contexts: If you need to access the values of REST framework's API settings in your project, you should use the api_settings object.
DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES ) The api_settings object will check for any user-defined settings, and otherwise fall back to the default values.

user_input: I just want the quickest possible auth to try my API from curl in early development. What's the simplest built-in scheme and what should I move off later?
reference: BasicAuthentication is simplest — it signs against username/password and is generally only appropriate for testing. Before production move to a stronger scheme (or at least serve only over https).
reference_contexts: Basic authentication is generally only appropriate for testing.
For example: WWW - Authenticate : Basic realm = "api" Note If you use BasicAuthentication in production you must ensure that your API is only available over https .
A list or tuple of authentication classes, that determines the default set of authenticators used when accessing the request.user or request.auth properties.

user_input: When an unauthenticated request is rejected I sometimes get 401 and sometimes 403. What actually decides which one DRF returns?
reference: It hinges on whether the first/highest-priority authentication class uses a WWW-Authenticate header: if it does, an unauthenticated denial is 401 with that header; if not, it's 403. A request that authenticated but lacked permission is always 403.
reference_contexts: The first authentication class set on the view is used when determining the type of response .
The request was not successfully authenticated, and the highest priority authentication class does not use WWW-Authenticate headers.
HTTP 401 Unauthorized HTTP 403 Permission Denied HTTP 401 responses must always include a WWW-Authenticate header, that instructs the client how to authenticate.
Signature: AuthenticationFailed(detail=None, code=None) Raised when an incoming request includes incorrect authentication.

user_input: I set permission_classes on a generic view but object-level checks don't run on my detail endpoint unless I use generics. When does DRF run object-level checks, and what do I do in my own view?
reference: Generic views run object-level permissions when .get_object() is called. In a custom view you must call self.check_object_permissions(request, obj) after retrieving the object, and note DRF's built-in classes (except DjangoObjectPermissions) don't implement has_object_permission unless you subclass them.
reference_contexts: Object level permissions are run by REST framework's generic views when .get_object() is called.

reference: It's intentional: all DRF views are opted out of LoginRequiredMiddleware, because DRF auth is decided by authentication/permission classes after the middleware runs, and redirecting API calls to a login page is wrong (a 401 is preferable). Enforce login via DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES and DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES instead.

REST framework offers an equivalent mechanism for DRF views via the global settings, DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES and DEFAULT_PERMISSION_CLASSES .

The view under test has SessionAuthentication in its authentication_classes. Nothing in my test touches middleware. Why does calling the view directly behave differently under DRF, and what's the right way to write these tests?
reference: In plain Django, CSRF validation runs in middleware, which isn't executed when you test views directly. In DRF it runs inside the view, so the request factory needs view-level CSRF checks disabled — use APIRequestFactory(enforce_csrf_checks=False) (the default) or authenticate with force_authenticate.
reference_contexts: When using REST framework, CSRF validation takes place inside the view, so the request factory needs to disable view-level CSRF checks.
CSRF validation in REST framework works slightly differently from standard Django due to the need to support both session and non-session based authentication to the same views.
